summary:
"Before the Smoke" is a community-focused platform that will help First Nations across Canada prepare for wildfires before they become emergencies.

Our website lets community members look up their First Nation to see the wildfire risk projected for the coming days, along with a clear explanation of what is driving it and practical advice on how to prepare. The platform also helps communities draft requests for firefighting personnel and equipment to submit to provincial governments and Indigenous Services Canada.

It combines NASA satellite fire detections and imagery (FIRMS and GIBS), 42 years of NASA POWER weather records, Canada's Fire Weather Index and wildfire reports, and Indigenous Services Canada's First Nations locations dataset.

First Nations represent approximately 5% of Canada's population, yet they account for around 42% of wildfire-related evacuation events. Our goal is to support earlier, community-driven preparedness rather than simply faster evacuation.

This is a prototype, not an official fire danger rating or alert service, and does not speak on behalf of any First Nation.
details:
What it does:

On our website, a user can search any First Nation (641 communities from ISC open data). They will see a map coloured by fire risk, the when they open one community page, they will get: a risk sentence for today and a look-ahead (1 day to 2 weeks); how sure we are and why; warning signs (heat, dry air, no soaking rain, wind, nearby satellite heat, thickening smoke); nearest reported wildfires and smoke; a built-in Q&A; and an “Ask for help” letter with official contacts. Nothing is sent by the site, the community copies, emails, or prints it.

How it works:

A transparent risk score (0–100) combines nine inputs, including Canada’s official Fire Weather Index (nearest reporting station, today + 2 days), humidity, rain, wind, temperature, vapour pressure deficit, soil moisture, nearby satellite heat, and a regional baseline. Cold/damp days are down-weighted; snow or frost scales the score down. Live mode uses real APIs and never invents numbers if a source fails. Example scenario mode shows a seeded summer day (14 July 2026, the week of real Thunder Bay–area evacuations) for demos; the NASA satellite photo for that date is real. Methods, limits, and source status are on/about.

Benefits:

Communities and the agencies they contact can work from one shared place, and requests for crews and equipment can go out earlier. Everything is explained in clear, everyday terms. In keeping with OCAP principles, the tool uses only publicly available locations, and it does not track visitors.

What we hope to achieve:

We hope to shift spending and attention toward preparedness, before a response is needed. Our next steps are to validate the score against fire records with Indigenous partners and to co-design governance with the communities the tool describes.

Tools:

TypeScript, Node.js/Express, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, Leaflet/React-Leaflet, Recharts. Hosted on Railway. Optional Anthropic Claude for free-form assistant answers; suggested questions use built-in rules and work offline.
